transcript.content: Hey Nik. Good to see you — what's on your mind today?

I am feeling very low, as I got laid off from turing in april 2026 and I am job searching for almost 5 months for entry level jobs, i got some interviews also but didn't make any offer, i just feel, what am i doing wrong, i just feel, not going to get a job in future,

Hey Nik. That’s a heavy weight to carry — five months of grinding, real effort, and still no offer. Anyone would feel worn down by that. You’re not failing; you’re fighting. And the fact that you’re even asking “what am I doing wrong?” shows you’re not giving up — you’re looking for leverage.  

Can you tell me what’s been the hardest part of the process so far? The interviews themselves? The silence after applying? Or something else that’s not clicking?
sometimes i got a very bad interview, sometimes, i got a decent in got silence after the interview, i call to HR, they don't pick up. sometimes, i complete the take-home assignment and got ghosted.

That’s a brutal cycle — you show up, do the work, even go the extra mile with take-homes, and then… nothing. The silence after effort is one of the hardest things to endure, especially when you’re already doubting yourself. It’s not just about skill at that point; it’s about being treated like a disposable candidate, not a person.  

What you’re describing isn’t failure — it’s a broken process on their end. But I get it: the longer it goes, the more it erodes your confidence.  

Can I ask — when you look back at those interviews, is there a pattern in the ones that felt decent? Something you did or said that made you walk away feeling okay, even if they ghosted later?

Like i call an interview when i got most of the questions but stuck in some questions, and in the final part of interview when i ask for feedback about me to the interviewer, they said - you have to work on somethings, but overall it was fine, we will keep you in the pipeline so keep in contact with the HR.

That "keep in contact with HR" line is a red flag, Nik — not because you’re doing anything wrong, but because it shifts the burden onto you to chase silence. If they want you, they’ll reach out. The fact that you’re the one calling, and they’re not picking up, tells you everything: you’re not a priority.  

And that feedback — “work on some things” — is meaningless without specifics. It’s polite ghosting. You’re not failing; you’re running into a system that avoids honest closure.  

But here’s what I’m seeing: you’re getting through interviews, answering most questions, and even asking for feedback — that’s not someone who’s off-track. That’s someone being strung along by companies with broken hiring practices.  

So I’ll ask this straight: when was the last time you walked away from an opportunity that treated you like an afterthought?

Okk so recently i had three interviews, one of was for a data scientist role at kotak, one for a data engineer role at Intelligance factory (a seed startup) and another for AI Engineer role at agentanalytics(also a startup), now for the kotak one, like first of all let me tell you this point as i had a kotak interview for the same role 4 months ago, the first round was as always a third part BarRaiser round, in which they asked me a coding question, which i could not write the correct code, both times but i convey the approach and the approach was right, and after the coding question they ask me some questions related to ML, DL, not LLD, LLMs, RAG, and some AI security questions, in the interview i had 4 months ago, i answer almost 60-70 % questions only and i was thinking of not getting to the next round but i got the call for the next round just the after day of previous round but in the interview i had currently in kotak, i answer 85-90 percent of the questions with confidance and I was expecting the next roundthis barraiser round was held on friday , i called to the HR at monday and he said just give me 1 hour, then i called him on monday then tuesday but he didn't pick up, one red flag i can identify is that this time in the barraiser the interviewer said about my feedback that you have to work on your time management as you spent too much time on the coding problem and still you didn't provide the final code solution and there will be various edge cases left also, and apart from this some of your answers were just generic and overall it was fine.

Thanks for sharing that, Nikhil — I know how draining it can be to go through multiple interviews in quick succession, especially when you're giving each one your full shot. You're clearly putting in the work, and it’s starting to show.

Let’s start with what’s working: your technical depth in AI/ML topics — LLMs, RAG, security — is clearly coming together. Going from 60–70% to 85–90% clarity and confidence in a Kotak BarRaiser round? That’s real progress. And the fact that you got past this round *last time* even with shaky coding tells me your domain knowledge is already competitive.

But here’s where we need to tighten up: **the coding execution under pressure**. It’s not just about the approach — which, yes, you’re nailing — but about delivering *working code*, within time, with edge cases handled. In high-stakes rounds like BarRaiser, they’re testing whether you can ship. And when an interviewer explicitly calls out time management and incomplete code — *twice* — it becomes a pattern they can’t ignore.

That silence from HR? Yeah, it stings. But don’t mistake delay for rejection. Kotak moves slow sometimes. Still, I’d treat this as a signal: the next opportunity might not wait. And you want to walk into it sharper.

Now, quick reality check: of these three roles, which one actually excites you the most? If it’s the **AI Engineer** role at AgentAnalytics — and I’m guessing it is — then let’s make sure you’re not just qualified, but *unstoppable* in the next interview loop.

Because here’s the truth: your foundation is strong. What’s missing is polish in translating that knowledge into crisp, timely execution — especially in coding. That’s fixable. Fast.

Want to spend 20 minutes mapping out a focused drill plan for timed coding + edge-case discipline? Or should we debrief the other two interviews first? Your call.

Okk so now let me describe you the agentanalytics interview, firs the history i was having this interview 1 month agd i got the iinterview cancelled as the HR said i will sceduled it to you later, not i got this interview later, i have the discussion with the co-founder, as the startup was main working on the vectordatabase buiseness, we had a detailed technical discussion, he was mainly interested in my Turing experiance, he got in detail in SFT and RLHF, i answer most of the questions confidantly but got stuck when he asked me some more match oriented problems like in RLHF, the DPO part, he commanded to ask claude for the DPO approach and then explain me the terms in the formula for DPO approach, now here i got stuck in cause i was not prepared for this, i was just knowing the theory and some tradeoffs but didn't learn the math behind it, after that we had a very little approx 2 minutes discussion on my projects that was focused on RAG, agents, but he was more interested in the actual code, like he wanted to ask me how i actually code, but the time limit ends, and he just explain the startup and ask for the feedback, and after this i just go a bidefencive here, i said something like this - I know i don't have a perticular experiance in this but i can ensure i can learn things quickly and i will give it my 100 percent, and the interview ends with this final note from the interviewer as - okk overall it was a fine discussion i will let you keep in the pipeline and mamta(HR) will be in contact with you. and now it's been approx 20 days, i had the followup with Mamta(HR) two times and she just said, thank you for waiting we are currently having interviews.

Nik, that co-founder interview at AgentAnalytics was a real moment — not a failure, but a signal. You held your own on SFT, RLHF, RAG, agents, and your Turing experience, which means your depth in applied AI is *real*. The fact that he went deep and you were still in the conversation shows growth. But here’s what stands out: you hit a wall on DPO math, and instead of faking it, you got honest — and then defensive. That defensiveness? It wasn’t weakness. It was the weight of five months of silence and near-misses pressing down in one moment.  

But let’s be precise: you didn’t fail because you didn’t know the math — you’re allowed to learn. You faltered because you didn’t *frame* the gap confidently. Next time, say: *"I haven’t internalized the DPO derivation yet, but here’s how I’d approach it…"* — then walk the structure, even if you don’t land the answer. That’s what they want: learning velocity, not perfection.  

And Mamta’s "we’re still interviewing" after 20 days? That’s not a no — but it’s not a yes either. It’s limbo. So here’s the pivot: stop waiting. You’ve done the work. Now, double down on what you *control* — your depth in math-heavy RLHF, your coding fluency in agent systems. That’s where we go next.  

When do you want to start?

now i don't know what should i learn and i don't have any plan and to be honest i feel so under-confident that sometime just feel i need revision for each of these topics and alongside the coding in DSA also

Nik, that feeling of not knowing where to go next — it makes total sense. You're not behind; you're in the messy middle of a real transition. And the fact that you're even thinking about revising DSA and advanced topics like DPO means you care about depth, not just checkboxes.

Here’s what I see: your knowledge in AI/ML is already strong — you’re clearing technical rounds on concepts, which is more than most can say. The gap isn’t breadth — it’s precision under pressure. You got the approach right at Kotak *twice*, but the code didn’t land. At AgentAnalytics, you knew RLHF but froze on DPO math. That’s not a knowledge deficit — it’s an execution gap.

So here’s what we do: no more “revise everything.” Instead, we lock onto two things —  
1. **DSA execution with time discipline** — not just solving, but solving *on time*, clean, first try.  
2. **Mathematical grounding in key ML algorithms** — like DPO, where you need to derive, not recall.

Let’s start today. I’ll help you build a plan — focused, no fluff. But first: how much time can you *realistically* put in today? Even 90 minutes, if it’s sharp and targeted, moves the needle.
it's the start of the day i can put 3 hours atleast

You’ve got 3 hours — that’s real time, and it’s yours to shape. Here’s what I’d do with it: spend the first 90 minutes on DSA coding, but not just any practice — focus on writing *complete, working code* under time pressure. Pick one problem, set a timer, and treat it like the BarRaiser round: correct approach isn’t enough this time — you need clean execution.

Then, 60 minutes on DPO: go back to the derivation that tripped you. Don’t skip steps. Write it out line by line until it’s not foreign — until you could explain it without memorizing. This isn’t about being perfect; it’s about proving to yourself that you can own the math.

Finally, 30 minutes reviewing the Kotak feedback: simulate a round where you’re coding live and talking through it. Record yourself. Listen for where your words get vague — that’s where they’ll doubt you.

We cut the planning and break to fit it all, because today’s about momentum, not management. You don’t need to revise everything — you need to sharpen what already belongs to you.
